newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba sees public authorities 97 deficit above plan.
newsitem.headline: Buba sees public authorities 97 deficit above plan.

text.p: Germany's federal, regional and municipal budget deficits are likely to exceed the government's plans for 1997 but the social insurance system should swing to surplus, the Bundesbank said on Wednesday.

Social insurance -- comprising pensions, unemployment, health and nursing insurance -- is counted as part of the public sector budget and is therefore relevant to Bonn's chances to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The Bundesbank noted in its June monthly report that the official tax estimate published in May showed the government had to cope with substantial revenue shortfalls in 1997.
The bank also said unemployment this year was likely to be "significantly higher" than envisaged at the end of 1996.
But it added that tax revenues had partly been squeezed by special factors in the opening months of 1997 and were likely to become less unfavourable during the rest of the year.
The bank did not predict the overall public sector deficit for 1997 which under the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria must not exceed three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

"...the deficits of the federal, regional and municipal authorities will probably exceed the planned levels," the bank's report said. "The foreseeable decline in the deficits could therefore lag behind expectations."
"By contrast the financial position of the social insurance systems should develop more positively than that of the ...public authorities," the report said.

The Bundesbank said the social insurance system was likely to return to a surplus in 1997 after running up a total deficit of 13 billion marks in 1996. The swing was explained by an increase in pension contributions, the bank said.

Looking ahead to 1998, the report said the public sector would have to intensify efforts to limit state consumption spending to achieve the goals of reducing the public deficit, cutting corporate taxation and reforming the tax system.

In the 1997 first quarter, the federal budget, together with the budgets of the federal states and special government funds like the Inherited Debt Redemption Fund, had a combined deficit of 34.5 billion marks, up 8.5 billion marks from the year-earlier period, the report said.
The figures do not include municipalities for which no data are yet available.
The main reason for the increased deficit was disappointing tax revenues. But the shortfall was partly explained by one-off factors in the opening months of 1997, the bank report said.
"...the revenues should during the further course of the year not develop quite as unfavourably as in the initial months of the year which were influenced by special factors," the report said.
First-quarter tax revenues excluding income from municipal taxes fell by more than four percent year-on-year in the first quarter.
That shortfall was partly caused by a shortening of payment periods for petrol tax and spirits tax which caused a three-billion mark jump in revenues from those taxes at the end of last year.

There was also barely any revenue yet from an increase in the real estate transfer tax and the reform of inheritance tax, both of which came into force at the start of 1997, while the scrapping of wealth tax had an immediate effect, the bank said.
Income tax revenues fell by three percent in the first quarter due in part to an increase in child benefit.

The federal budget developed more unfavourably than budgets of other public authorities, running up a deficit of just under 30 billion marks in the first quarter, up 10 billion marks from the year-earlier period.

Federal tax revenues fell by 7.5 percent in the period while federal outlays rose by just under four percent, driven higher in part by a 12 percent increase in unemployment benefit payments as joblessness rose, the bank said.
